title: Counting it loss (Philippians 3:1–11)
hookLine: everything Paul was proud of, he counts as loss compared with knowing Christ

cards: A résumé, printed on the good paper. Born into the right family. The best teachers.
A record nobody can fault. Then the owner takes a red pen and writes across the whole page: loss. Not shredding it.
Not lying about it. Just marking it down, as if the numbers had been in the wrong column all along. That's close to what Paul does in the third chapter of Philippians.
He lays out every credential he had, then moves the whole list to the other side of the ledger.

teach.b: Here's the list, in the King James Bible: "Circumcised the eighth day, of the stock of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, an Hebrew of the Hebrews; as touching the law, a Pharisee."

He kept the law of his people with great zeal, and says that by its measure of righteousness he was blameless. He isn't mocking any of it. These are real goods: an honored family, a faithful upbringing, a serious life.
"But what things were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ." It's bookkeeping language: gain and loss.

Then he goes further: "I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord." All things. And he uses a rough word for them, one that means refuse, the scraps you throw out.
Older English Bibles put it bluntly as dung. Why so strong?

teach.h: TO KNOW HIM, NOT A RECORD.
teach.b: Because what he wants now is not a record but a person: "That I may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings." Know, here, is not knowing about. It's the way you know a friend.
Christians read this passage in different ways. Some hear a conversion from one way of standing before God to another.

teach.h: I COUNT ALL THINGS BUT LOSS.
teach.b: Others stress that Paul never stops being a Jew, and that what he counts as loss is his own standing, his pride, not the Torah or his people. Both readings see the turn: the things that once defined him no longer get to.

how: Many Christians read Philippians 3 when thinking about pride and identity, and some churches use verses 7 to 11 in Lent as a reflection on what to set aside.

o: a Roman official who governed a province
a priest who offered sacrifices in the Temple
a member of a Jewish group devoted to the law

games.q: what's inside Philippians 3:1–11 — tap the pairs.

s: Paul says his upbringing and law-keeping were worthless all along
he lists them as real gains, then counts them as loss compared with knowing Christ.
Paul uses the language of bookkeeping
gain and loss, as if moving items from one column to the other.
the KJV renders Paul's rough word as dung
the Greek means refuse or scraps; the KJV says dung.

games.q: you're Paul. you have the family, the training and a spotless record. what do you do with it?
o: lead with it, so people trust you.
count it all as loss compared with knowing Christ.
games.why: "what things were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ." he doesn't hide the list. he re-files it.

practice: Name something you're proud of that quietly runs your life: a title, a grade, being the one who's always right, or always busy, or always fine.

It may be a real good, as Paul's were, so don't throw it away; just picture writing it on a card and moving it out of the center, and notice what's left in the middle. If you pray, you can hand it to God and leave the card there.

wordCard.voice: Pharisee. Paul's own credential before his bookkeeping turn: a label he moved, with everything else he had, into the loss column, next to knowing Christ.

orig.note: Greek: loss, damage, a business write-off. Paul uses it in verses 7 and 8.

carryVoice: Your line: all else is loss. A record, traded for a person. That's day six hundred sixty-three.
